conventions: Body maps: north is at the top and east longitude increases to the right. centerLongitudeDeg is the east longitude at the image center (null = unknown or not meaningful). For a point at east longitude L and latitude B: u = 0.5 + (L - centerLongitudeDeg) / 360 (modulo 1, from the left edge), v = (90 - B) / 180 (from the top edge). latitudeType says which latitude B is: 'planetocentric' or 'planetographic'. The two types differ for a flattened body only. An entry with no latitudeType has no statement of the source about it. Where a longitude note says 'found by inspection' or 'check by inspection', the check is good to a few degrees only. Star map: right ascension 0 h is at the image center and right ascension increases to the left; declination +90 degrees is at the top. For right ascension A and declination D in degrees: u = 0.5 - A / 360 (modulo 1, from the left edge), v = (90 - D) / 180 (from the top edge). Coverage: 'partial' means that a large part of the surface has no image data. In most of these files that part is black (21 to 68 percent of the surface); Deimos has light gray blank areas instead. The maps of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the exception: the build fills their areas with no image data (7 to 31 percent of the surface) with a zonal mean color, and the fields latitudeLimitsDeg, filledBands and filledSharePercent describe the fill. filledSharePercent is the filled share of the surface of a sphere. A map with 'global' coverage can still have small black gaps (4.2 percent of the surface or less in these files); the note of the entry describes them. latitudeLimitsDeg gives [south, north]: the map has image data only between these two latitudes. For Jupiter the source itself fills the areas beyond these limits with a flat color. colour: 'natural' = the source calls the image natural color; 'near natural' = the image comes from filters for visible light, but it is not an exact copy of what the eye sees; 'enhanced' = false color (the image uses light that the eye cannot see, or it makes color differences stronger); 'grey' = one filter only. An entry with no colour field has no such class in this work. The fields filters and observed come from the source. Ring strip: the left edge is at innerRadiusKm and the right edge is at outerRadiusKm from the center of the planet. The radius is linear along the strip. See the note of the entry saturn_ring.
sourcesNote: Each map comes from the data of a space mission, of a telescope or of star catalogs.
No map comes from an application of a company or from the web site of a person.
Six maps come from the JPL Solar System Simulator, an application of NASA.
They are the maps of Deimos, Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon.
The JPL page shows that the USGS made these six maps from images of Viking and Voyager.
The catalog of USGS Astrogeology has no image mosaic of these six bodies.

The source says that each pixel is the average of all images that meet its criteria, and that the reflectance is corrected to one lighting geometry. Near both poles the map shows strong shading and stretched pixels. No seam is visible at the left and right edge. The original file has 23040 x 11520 pixels.

textures.title: OPAL Saturn Cycle 32, rotation A (2025a): color global map from the filters F631N, F502N and F395N
textures.longitudeNote: Readme of the source (hlsp_opal_hst_wfc3-uvis_saturn-2025_all_v1_readme.txt): 'left edge = 360 System III W. longitude, decreasing to the right'. West longitude decreases to the right, so east longitude increases to the right. The left edge is at 0 degrees and the image center is at 180 degrees east (System III). Clouds move with the wind: a cloud keeps its longitude only for a short time.
textures.filters: red = F631N, green = F502N, blue = F395N (Hubble WFC3/UVIS), with slight contrast enhancement by the source. The number in the name of a Hubble filter is its wavelength in nanometers.
textures.note: Hubble Space Telescope map of 29 August 2025 (OPAL program). The source page calls this file 'RotA Color Preview'. The readme gives for the first rotation: 'Rotation 1 (Aug 29 05:53:28 to 14:20:17 UT)'. Clouds change with time. The readme says: 'Color maps (TIFF only), are generated from the F631N (red), F502N (green), and F395N (blue) filters, with slight contrast enhancement.' So the color is near natural, not exact: the blue channel is violet light of 395 nm. The latitude is planetographic (readme: 'between -90 and +90 deg planetographic latitude', with 'equatorial and polar radii of 60268 and 54364 km'). With these radii the planetographic latitude is larger than the planetocentric latitude by up to 5.9 degrees. The source removes the limb darkening of each image (readme: 'Minnaert correction'). So the map has no day side and no night side. The readme says: 'seams between maps were interpolated to smooth, where needed' and 'ARTIFACTS: Multiple moons (and their shadows) can be seen crossing the mosaics.' The original file has no image data near the poles and in a band near the equator: these areas are black, and each has a dark ragged border. The readme does not explain the band near the equator. My reading: the rings and their shadow hide the planet there. The build treats the borders as no data too. So the image data cover 75.2 degrees north to 82.2 degrees south, without the band from 5.4 degrees north to 0.6 degrees south. The build fills the rest (7.4 percent of the surface of a sphere): see the fields latitudeLimitsDeg and filledBands. The fill is not an observation. Inspection of the small image: the map shows pale bands. They are pink-gray in the north, bright yellow-white at the equator and green-gray in the south. A blue-gray band lies near 67 degrees south. The valid rows get darker and browner toward both limits, so the fill at both poles is brown. My reading: these rows lie near the edge of the disc in the Hubble images. A faint red-brown vertical stripe lies at about 17 percent of the width, mostly in the north. My reading: it is a seam between two images of the source. A faint red-brown smudge remains at this place at both fill limits. The map has a few small dark dots and bright dots (moons and their shadows, by the readme). No seam is visible at the left and right edge: the two edges differ by 1 of 255 on average. The original file has 1800 x 900 pixels (5 pixels per degree): the published image is not sharper than the original.

textures.title: Panoramic Rings (PIA06175)
textures.author: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute
textures.longitudeNote: A ring strip has no longitude. The horizontal axis is the distance from the center of Saturn.
textures.filters: red, green and blue filters of the Cassini narrow-angle camera (the source calls the image a natural color mosaic)

ring.radiusSource: Table of the NASA NSSDC Saturnian Rings Fact Sheet (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/satringfact.html, last update 19 April 2022): 'C inner edge' 74,658 km and 'A outer edge' 136,780 km. The caption of the image gives the same outer radius: 'from a radius of 74,565 kilometers to 136,780 kilometers'. The radius of each calibration feature comes from the same table. The table says: 'Rings, ringlets and gaps of width less than 1000 km are listed by inner edge radius.'
ring.alphaSource: Brightness of the image (largest color channel), divided by the largest brightness of the strip. It is not occultation data and not a measured optical depth.
ring.colourSource: Mean color of the image over 9 columns (about 98 km) around each pixel, scaled to the largest brightness of the strip. The mean removes the color fringes of the image at sharp ring edges.

textures.note: PNG with transparency (straight alpha, not premultiplied). The horizontal axis is the distance from the center of Saturn: the left edge is at 74,658 km (inner edge of the C ring) and the right edge is at 136,780 km (outer edge of the A ring). The radius is linear along the strip (30.33 km per pixel). All rows are equal. The strip comes from a Cassini mosaic of 12 December 2004 (PIA06175). The caption says: 'This mosaic of six images covers a distance of approximately 62,000 kilometers along the ring plane, from a radius of 74,565 kilometers to 136,780 kilometers (46,333 to 84,991 miles) from the planet's center.' and 'This view is from Cassini's vantage point beneath the ring plane. The rings are tilted away from Cassini at an angle of about 4 degrees.' and 'Images taken using red, green and blue spectral filters were used to create this natural color mosaic.' Alpha is the brightness of the image and not a measured opacity (field alphaSource). The color of each pixel times its alpha value gives the brightness of the image again. The color is a mean over 9 columns of the image (field colourSource): in the image the blue channel is less sharp than the red and green channels, and this makes color fringes at sharp ring edges. Inspection of the strip: it shows the C ring (alpha about 0.1 to 0.5), the B ring (0.6 to 0.95), the Cassini division (0.05 to 0.6) and the A ring (0.5 to 0.65) with the Encke gap and the Keeler gap. The color is warm tan in the B ring, pale pink in the A ring and lavender in the C ring and in the Cassini division: the image has these colors. The gaps are not fully clear: their alpha is 0.02 to 0.05. The image has a brightness of 5 to 9 of 255 in the gaps and of 1 to 3 in the sky just outside of the A ring. My reading: this is stray light. The caption does not say which face of the rings the image shows. The dense B ring is the brightest part of the image. So my reading is: the image shows the sunlit face. The strip has no D ring and no F ring: the image does not show them. Radius scale: the build fits a straight line to five sharp ring edges of the fact sheet (field radiusFit). These five edges agree with the fit to 5 km. Three other features differ from the fact sheet by 45 km to 88 km: the inner edge of the Maxwell ringlet, the inner edge of the B ring (a slow rise in the image) and the inner edge of the A ring (a small step in the image). So a ring feature can lie up to about 90 km (3 pixels) from its true place. The fit gives 10.87 km per pixel of the original image. The caption says: 'The image scale is 10.5 kilometers (6.5 miles) per pixel.' By the fit the image starts at 74,699 km. So the first pixel of the large strip has no image data: its alpha value is 0.

textures.note: Monochrome (gray) Dawn mosaic (framing camera, clear filter, high altitude mapping orbit). The source says that the images of one cycle make the mosaic, 'to have similar viewing and illumination conditions'. The surface shows the shading and the shadows of that lighting. Inspection of the small image: the area near the north pole is black or very dark (2.7 percent of the surface is black). The source does not explain it. My reading: this area had no sunlight when Dawn took these images. Craters in the north have long shadows. The rows at the south pole are smeared. No seam is visible at the left and right edge. The source says: 'At the original edge when wrapped a nodata line was pushed into the mosaic. This was covered using a couple neighboring pixels for artistic purposes only.' The source says that the map projection uses a sphere of 255 km radius. The source calls the file 'preliminary'. The original file has 26704 x 13352 pixels.

The source says: 'Images were photometrically normalized to 30° phase angle using a Minneart model.' and 'Overlaps were masked along natural feature boundaries for a nearly seamless result.' The file is the 8-bit version. The source says: 'The mapping used to convert to 8bit was a linear stretch from 0.0 - 0.044 to 1 - 254, maintaining 0 as NoDATA.' Inspection of the small image: the map shows dark rubble with boulders and their small shadows. Ragged strips at both poles are black: they have no data (4.2 percent of the surface). A lighter band lies near the equator. No seam is visible at the left and right edge. The projection uses a sphere of 250 m radius. Bennu is not a sphere: the map does not fit a sphere exactly. The original file has 31417 x 15709 pixels (5 cm per pixel).

textures.filters: filter 4 of the NEAR Multispectral Imager (950 nm)
textures.licenceStatement: USGS record of this data set: 'Access Constraints: None', 'Use Constraints: Please cite authors'. The record does not use the words 'public domain'. textures.note: Monochrome (gray) albedo map from NEAR Shoemaker images (Multispectral Imager, filter 4) in near-infrared light (950 nm). The source says that most images of the mission use this filter. The map shows albedo: the source corrects the images 'to 0 degrees phase (0 deg incidence, 0 deg emission)'. So the map has little shading. Inspection of the small image: the map shows a gray surface with bright crater walls. Two large bright features lie near 20 percent and near 75 percent of the width. The rows near both poles are smeared. The map has no black area. The original has scattered single black pixels with the value 0 (0.06 percent of its pixels). My reading: they have no data. Its last column has 272 of them and its first column has 83: after a plain resize they make a thin dark broken line at the left and right edge. So the build fills these pixels in the first 8 and the last 8 columns (582 pixels): see the field changes. After this repair no seam is visible at the left and right edge. The file is the browse image (8-bit PNG) of the data file eros_nearmsi_filter4.tif (32-bit). The archive does not say how it scales the values to 8 bits. The projection uses a sphere of 17 km radius. Eros is very far from a sphere: the map does not fit a sphere. The original file has 10682 x 5341 pixels (10 m per pixel).

The code calculates the light of the Sun on the oceans. The project removed the earlier map of the oceans, because the project uses no file from a different application.
The project removed the earlier normal map, because the project uses no file from a different application. The project did not search for a different normal map.

The project searched USGS Astrogeology, NASA Photojournal, NASA 3D Resources and Wikimedia Commons for a color map of the haze of Titan. It found no color map of the haze from the data of a mission with a clear license. NASA 3D Resources has a map of Titan, but the JPL page gives this name to that map: "Fictitious Titan concept". The file `titan_surface.jpg` shows the surface in near-infrared light.
